\title{Correctness-Gated Policy Optimization for\\
High-Frequency DSP Accelerator RTL}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Functional correctness alone does not distinguish slow register-transfer level
(RTL) from hardware that closes timing at a useful clock. We train a generator
with a correctness-gated physical objective: an input/output-equivalence oracle
first rejects incorrect modules, and a learned frequency proxy ranks only those
that pass. The proxy is used for training but never as an evaluation result.
Evaluation instead joins the original sample multiplicities to real post-route
Vivado measurements and assigns zero frequency to every incorrect or
implementation-failed sample. On a split frozen before training, covering
\claim{DesignCount} designs from \claim{FamilyCount} accelerator families, this
equal-sample endpoint rises from \claim{InterpSftPenalized} to
\claim{InterpGrpoPenalized}~MHz under parameter interpolation and from
\claim{ExtrapSftPenalized} to \claim{ExtrapGrpoPenalized}~MHz under
extrapolation. The paired gain is positive for \claim{OverallImproved} of
\claim{DesignCount} designs. One optimized draw matches an idealized perfect
selector over approximately \claim{InterpEquivalentDraws} supervised draws in
interpolation and \claim{ExtrapEquivalentDraws} in extrapolation. A bounded
trajectory audit also catches reward overoptimization: late proxy reward rises
from \claim{TrajectoryLateProxy} to \claim{TrajectoryFinalProxy}~MHz while
conditional measured frequency changes from \claim{TrajectoryLateConditional}
to \claim{TrajectoryFinalConditional}~MHz and equal-sample measured frequency
falls. The result is therefore a measured policy-distribution shift toward fast,
correct implementations, not evidence that the learned proxy is itself an
accurate evaluator.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
RTL generation, reinforcement learning, large language models, FPGA,
design space exploration, reward hacking
\end{IEEEkeywords}
